title: upekkha
hook: upekkha; the steady mind in a storm
carry: let it be as it is

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Jataka, the monkey king. Your line was the bridge he made of his body. Did you thank someone who was a bridge for you? Day nineteen.
screen: `THE JATAKA — THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Monday, the boss calls the work brilliant, and the whole day floats. Tuesday, a client calls it the worst thing they've seen, and sleep won't come. Wednesday, a friend forgets a birthday. Thursday, a stranger compliments a coat, and suddenly it's fine again. Up, down, up, down, like a boat in weather. Plenty of weeks go like that, and it gets called being human. It is. But the Buddha named those winds, one by one, and taught a way to stand in them without being blown over. Today, the steady mind in a storm.
screen: `MONDAY: BRILLIANT.` → `TUESDAY: THE WORST.` → `A BOAT IN WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Upekkha. Equanimity. It's the fourth of the divine abodes you met with karuna: friendliness, compassion, gladness, and this. The word comes from a root meaning to look, with a prefix meaning over or near. To look on, from a steady place. Not to look away. The Buddha named eight worldly conditions, four pairs, often pictured as winds. Gain and loss. Fame and disgrace. Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. The text says they come to everyone, the untaught and the wise alike. The winds aren't the problem. Getting flung around by them is. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, has the picture: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." A rock. The wind still blows. The rock still feels it. It just doesn't move. Here's the part of upekkha that's easy to get wrong. Equanimity isn't indifference. Buddhaghosa warned of its near enemy, a dull, unknowing calm that looks like it but isn't. Some teachers today call that indifference. Indifference says, I don't care. Equanimity says, I care, and I'm not going to be knocked over. It comes last of the four, and here's one way to see why. Metta wishes well. Karuna stays with pain. Mudita is glad for others. And upekkha keeps all of that steady, so the caring doesn't burn you out. A good nurse, a good parent, a good friend in an emergency. Warm, and calm. That's upekkha. Letting things be as they are, and still showing up.
screen: `UPEKKHA — LOOKING ON, STEADY.` · `EIGHT WORLDLY WINDS.` · `THE ROCK IN THE WIND.` · `NOT INDIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Sit tall and steady, like a rock on a hillside. Now let one wind blow: remember a moment of praise. Notice what it does in your body. Let it pass. Now let the other blow: a moment of blame. Notice that too. Let it pass. Come back to the breath, and to the weight of your body on the seat. The winds come and go. You stay. The bell holds the time.
Equanimity. Upekkha: looking on from a steady place, a rock in the eight winds. Caring, and not knocked over. Nineteenth word.
Your line: let it be as it is. Today, when praise or blame comes, take one breath before you react, and feel your feet on the ground. Day nineteen.

howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate upekkha as one of the four brahmaviharas, often after metta, karuna and mudita, by reflecting that beings meet the results of their own actions, and by practicing steadiness through life's gains and losses.

fork.setup: you get a glowing review at work, then harsh criticism the next day. according to the teaching on the eight winds, what's the goal?
options: feel both, and stay steady like a rock.
fork.reveal: the winds still blow, and the rock still feels them. it just isn't moved. equanimity isn't escaping the winds; it's standing in them.

original.note: Pali: equanimity, looking on. Sanskrit: upekṣā. The fourth brahmavihāra.

trapdoor: what you thought: staying calm by not caring.
what it means: a steady mind in the eight winds, praise and blame, gain and loss, that still cares.

what a scholar hears: upekkhā, from upa + ikkh, to look on. the Lokavipatti Sutta (AN 8.6) names the eight worldly conditions; Buddhaghosa names an unknowing, worldly equanimity as its near enemy, often glossed as indifference.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer tells the listener what they felt or claims 'most of us'; AN 8.6 names eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma), so 'winds' is now given as the picture, and 'everyone gets all eight' follows the sutta; Buddhaghosa's near enemy is unknowing equanimity, with 'indifference' credited to some teachers; cut 'the most important thing', the unsupported 'that's why it's last', and a 'Think of'.
Dhammapada 81 quoted from Max Müller (1881); confirm exact wording.
The index title is 'upekkha' and the word is 'equanimity'; kept as given.
Etymology upa + ikkh (to look): confirm the gloss 'to look on, from a steady place'.
Visuddhimagga: equanimity's near enemy is unknowing (worldly) equanimity, often explained as indifference. Confirm the simplification.
Mudita mentioned in passing (introduced on day 16).
